lesson_title: Crates, Balloons and Cordial: the Mole Decoded
hook_text: A warehouse never counts single eggs. Chemistry never counts single atoms. Meet the crate holding 602 000 000 000 000 000 000 000.
clip_script: No warehouse counts single eggs. Everything moves in crates, because the packers put the same number in every crate. Chemistry runs its warehouse with exactly one crate size for the entire universe: 6,02 times 10 to the 23 particles per crate. The crate is called a mole. Here is the warehouse insight that unlocks everything: a crate of ping-pong balls and a crate of cricket balls hold the same COUNT but weigh completely different amounts. Chemistry's crates behave identically. A crate of hydrogen atoms weighs 1 gram; a crate of sulphur dioxide molecules weighs 64 grams. That per-crate weight is the molar mass, and the periodic table is the warehouse ledger quoting it for every element. So when a question hands you grams and wants moles, it is really asking: how many full crates is this? Divide the mass by the crate weight. Gases are even simpler — at standard conditions every gas parks one crate in 22,4 cubic decimetres, because a gas is mostly empty space and only the count matters. Crates, balloons, cordial jugs. That is the whole chapter.
visual_style: A forklift stacking identical crates whose scale readouts differ wildly; two equal balloons over very different scales; a shot of syrup poured into a glass and then a jug, colours fading with volume.
mood: Brisk and liberating — the most feared number in chemistry reduced to warehouse logic.
pacing: Fast warehouse open, three tidy beats — crates, balloons, jugs — clean snap close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn every mole question into a two-step conversion.
